clean_summary:
Off-policy, value-based reinforcement learning methods like Q-learning are attractive because they can learn from any experience, including data from older policies or other agents. However, bootstrapping can lead to inaccuracies in long-horizon value estimates, which is a significant challenge in practice.

This work introduces n-step inequalities that improve the accuracy of value learning over long horizons. By leveraging these inequalities, the method enhances the stability and reliability of Q-learning, particularly in environments where long-term planning is essential. The practical implication is that this approach enables more effective learning from diverse experiences, ultimately improving the performance of reinforcement learning agents.

title: Chelsea Finn (@chelseabfinn)
summary:
2/ Student feedback is a fundamental problem in scaling education.
Providing good feedback is hard: existing approaches provide canned responses, cryptic error messages, or simply provide the answer.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/E6whjeBUcAAZJYI.jpg
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/E6whjfEVkAM6GKd.jpg
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/E6whjgCVgAEV7m6.jpg

title: Chelsea Finn (@chelseabfinn)
summary:
3/ Providing feedback is also hard for ML: not a ton of data, teachers frequently change their assignments, and student solutions are open-ended and long-tailed.
Supervised learning doesn’t work. We weren’t sure if this problem can even be solved using ML.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/E6wiLq0VUAMi-Np.jpg

title: Chelsea Finn (@chelseabfinn)
summary:
4/ But, we can frame it as a few-shot learning problem! Using data from past HWs and exams of Stanford’s intro CS course, we train a model to give feedback for a new problem with only ~20 examples.
Humans are critical to this process: instructors define a rubric & feedback text.

title: Chelsea Finn (@chelseabfinn)
summary:
5/ Because this is open-ended Python code, our base architecture is transformers + prototypical networks.
But, there are many important details for this to *actually* work: task augmentation, question & rubric text as side info, preprocessing, and code pre-training.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/E6wie0lUYAANjZ1.jpg

title: Chelsea Finn (@chelseabfinn)
summary:
6/ How well does this work?
In offline expts, meta-learning:
* achieves 8%-21% greater accuracy than supervised learning
* comes within 8% of a human TA on held-out exams.
Ablations show a >10% difference in accuracy with different design choices.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/E6wizxpUcAERxDL.png

title: Chelsea Finn (@chelseabfinn)
summary:
8/ We also did several checks for bias. Among the countries & gender identities with the most representation (i.e. largest statistical power), we see no signs of bias.
Not too surprising given the model only sees typed python code w/o comments, but super important to check.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/E6wjKFFVgAEY-x5.jpg

RL fine-tuning often prematurely collapses policy entropy.
We consider a general framework, called set RL, i.e. RL over a set of trajectories from a policy.
We use it to incentivize diverse solutions & optimize for inference time performance.
Paper:
Quoting @jubayer_hamid
Exploration is fundamental to RL. Yet policy gradient methods often collapse: during training they fail to explore broadly, and converge into narrow, easily exploitable behaviors. The result is poor generalization, limited gains from test-time scaling, and brittleness on tasks where strategic exploration is necessary. We introduce a framework for training a policy over sets of generations and use it to induce exploration.
Work with @ifdita_hasan (co-lead), @ellenjxu_ , @chelseabfinn and @DorsaSadigh at Stanford 🧵

This creates a fundamental mismatch between how we ultimately deploy these systems and how we train them, leaving much of search and synthesis unoptimized.

clean_summary:
Pretraining a Q-function often doesn’t actually help reinforcement learning finetuning, compared to initializing Q from scratch. The key is that pretraining Q-functions on data from diverse policies is essential to see improvements from pretraining.
